claim_excerpt:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The named **pentagon curve** is an unconditional instance of the calculation below. Its smooth projective model is
$$X_0:=\{[Z_0:\cdots:Z_4]\in\mathbb P^4(\mathbb C):Z_1^2=Z_0Z_2,\ Z_1Z_2=Z_0Z_3,\ Z_2^2=Z_1Z_3,\ Z_4^2=Z_2Z_3-Z_0^2\}.$$
The affine chart is $[1:x:x^2:x^3:y]$ with $y^2=x^5-1$, and there is a unique point at infinity. This compact connected curve has genus two; $T_0(x,y)=(\zeta x,y)$, $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/5}$, has order five and $y$ is its degree-five quotient to the sphere, branched at $\pm i,\infty$. It is biholomorphic to two opposite regular pentagons with parallel sides glued by translation, with $T_0$ induced by their rotation. The oriented real-$y$ sheet
$$C_0:\quad x=(1+y^2)^{1/5},\qquad -\infty\le y\le+\infty,$$
has both endpoints at infinity; its classes $C_0,T_0C_0,T_0^2C_0,T_0^3C_0$ are an **integral** homology basis, and their five-orbit sum is zero. All these witness claims are proved locally below ([[def-complex-projective-space-and-holomorphic-charts]]).

More generally, let $X$ be a compact
connected Riemann surface of genus $2$ admitting an automorphism $T$ of order
$5$, with $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$ a free rank-one module over
$A:=\mathbb Z[T]/(1+T+T^2+T^3+T^4)$ generated by a class $C$, and suppose there
is a degree-five quotient map $y:X\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$ whose fibres are the
$T$-orbits (in particular the constructed $X_0,T_0,C_0$ above). Then:

1. The eigenvalues of $T^{*}$ on $\Omega(X)\cong\mathbb C^2$
([[lem-holomorphic-differentials-form-a-g-dimensional-space]]) are primitive
fifth roots of unity; after replacing $T$ by a power and choosing the basis,
there is a basis $\omega_1,\omega_2$ of $\Omega(X)$ with
$T^{*}\omega_i=\zeta^{i}\omega_i$ for $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/5}$ and
$P(C,\omega_i)=1$, $i=1,2$
([[def-period-pairing-and-period-lattice]]).
2. On the cycle $T^{k}C$ one has $P(T^{k}C,\omega_i)=\zeta^{ki}$, so the period
lattice is the rank-four lattice
$$\Lambda=\bigl\{\bigl(p(\zeta),p(\zeta^2)\bigr):p\in\mathbb Z[T]\bigr\} =\bigl\{(a,\sigma(a)):a\in\mathbb Z[\zeta]\bigr\}\subseteq\mathbb C^2,$$
$\sigma$ the Galois conjugation $\zeta\mapsto\zeta^{2}$, and
$\operatorname{Jac}(X)=\mathbb C^{2}/\Lambda$
([[def-jacobian-of-a-compact-riemann-surface]]).
3. The period vectors of the four cycles $C,TC,T^2C,T^3C$ are the four columns
$(1,1),(\zeta,\zeta^2),(\zeta^2,\zeta^4),(\zeta^3,\zeta)$, which generate
$\Lambda$; they are $\mathbb R$-linearly independent, because a real relation
$\sum_kx_k(\zeta^k,\zeta^{2k})=0$ gives $\sum_kx_k\zeta^{jk}=0$ for
$j=1,2,3,4$ (using conjugation for $j=3,4$) and the Vandermonde matrix
$(\zeta^{jk})_{1\le j\le4,\,0\le k\le3}$ has trivial kernel: a polynomial of
degree at most three with four distinct roots is zero
([[thm-root-bound-for-polynomials-over-a-domain]]). Define the real $4\times4$
matrix $M$ by its columns
$$M_{:,k+1}:=(\operatorname{Re}\zeta^k,\operatorname{Im}\zeta^k,\operatorname{Re}\zeta^{2k},\operatorname{Im}\zeta^{2k})^{\mathsf T},\qquad 0\le k\le3.$$
Here $(z_1,z_2)\in\mathbb C^2$ has real coordinates
$(\operatorname{Re}z_1,\operatorname{Im}z_1,\operatorname{Re}z_2,\operatorname{Im}z_2)$.
Hence $\Lambda$ is a full lattice of covolume $|\det M|>0$, so the
period torus is compact ([[def-full-rank-lattice-covolume-and-dual-lattice]],
[[thm-riemann-bilinear-relations]]).
4. Every point of $\operatorname{Jac}(X)$ is represented by a degree-zero
divisor and $\operatorname{Pic}^0(X)\cong\operatorname{Jac}(X)$
([[thm-jacobi-inversion]]).
supplier_reference_lines: [F7] A nonzero polynomial of degree $n$ over an integral domain has at most $n$ distinct roots ([[thm-root-bound-for-polynomials-over-a-domain]]). A square matrix with trivial kernel is invertible ([[thm-invertible-matrix-theorem]]).

claim_excerpt:
Let $n\ge1$, let $q$ be a prime power, put $G=\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$ and let $V=\mathbb F_q^n$ carry the standard flag $V_0\subsetneq V_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq V_n=V$ ([[def-standard-subgroups-of-gl-n-over-a-finite-field]]). Let $\alpha=(a_1,\dots,a_r)$ and $\beta=(b_1,\dots,b_s)$ be compositions of $n$ with blocks $I_1,\dots,I_r$ and $J_1,\dots,J_s$ and partial sums $d_i=a_1+\cdots+a_i$, $e_j=b_1+\cdots+b_j$ ([[def-compositions-partial-flags-and-standard-parabolics]]), let $P_\alpha\ge B$ and $P_\beta\ge B$ be the corresponding standard parabolics, let $W_\alpha,W_\beta\le W\cong S_n$ be the parabolic Weyl subgroups and let $\ell$ be the inversion length ([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). For $\tau\in S_n$ put $$M(\tau)_{ij}:=\#\{\,v\in J_j:\tau(v)\in I_i\,\}\qquad(1\le i\le r,\ 1\le j\le s),$$ the **block-count matrix** of $\tau$, a matrix with nonnegative integer entries, and call $\tau$ **$(\alpha,\beta)$-block-increasing** when $\tau$ is increasing on each $\beta$-block ($v<v'$ in a common $J_j$ implies $\tau(v)<\tau(v')$) and $\tau^{-1}$ is increasing on each $\alpha$-block ($u<u'$ in a common $I_i$ implies $\tau^{-1}(u)<\tau^{-1}(u')$). For $x\in G$ let $\sigma(x)\in S_n$ be its Bruhat index, the unique permutation with $x\in BP_{\sigma(x)}B$ ([[thm-bruhat-decomposition-of-gl-n-over-a-finite-field]]). Then:

1. **Double cosets.** The assignment $\Psi\bigl(W_\alpha w_\tau W_\beta\bigr):=P_\alpha P_\tau P_\beta$ is a well-defined bijection from the set of $(W_\alpha,W_\beta)$-double cosets of $W$ onto the set of $(P_\alpha,P_\beta)$-double cosets of $G$.
2. **Block counts are a complete invariant.** For all $x,y\in G$ one has $M(\sigma(x))=M(\sigma(y))$ if and only if $P_\alpha xP_\beta=P_\alpha yP_\beta$, if and only if $W_\alpha\sigma(x)W_\beta=W_\alpha\sigma(y)W_\beta$; and $\tau\mapsto M(\tau)$ induces a bijection from $W_\alpha\backslash W/W_\beta$ onto the set of all matrices with nonnegative integer entries whose row sums are $a_1,\dots,a_r$ and whose column sums are $b_1,\dots,b_s$.
3. **Unique minimal representative.** Every $(W_\alpha,W_\beta)$-double coset contains exactly one $(\alpha,\beta)$-block-increasing permutation, and this permutation is the unique element of the coset of minimal inversion length; every other element of the coset has strictly larger length. It is the **monotone matching** determined by $M$: as the elements of a fixed $\beta$-block $J_j$ are listed in increasing order, their images run in increasing order through the first $M_{1j}$ elements of $I_1$ not already allocated to $J_1,\dots,J_{j-1}$, then through the first $M_{2j}$ such elements of $I_2$, and so on, the blocks $J_1,J_2,\dots,J_s$ being processed in this order.
supplier_reference_lines: [L8] For $A\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$ the map $v\mapsto Av$ is a linear isomorphism of $V$ ([[thm-invertible-matrix-theorem]]), hence injective; therefore for every linear subspace $U\le V$ the restriction of this map to $U$ is an injective linear map $U\to V$ with image $A[U]$, and a linear map whose domain $U$ is finite-dimensional satisfies $\dim_{\mathbb F_q}U=\dim_{\mathbb F_q}\ker+\dim_{\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{im}$, so that $\dim_{\mathbb F_q}A[U]=\dim_{\mathbb F_q}U$; a linear isomorphism of finite-dimensional spaces preserves dimension ([[thm-rank-nullity]], [[cor-finite-dimensional-vector-spaces-are-isomorphic-iff-equal-dimension]], [[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

claim_excerpt:
Let $n\ge1$, let $q$ be a prime power and put $G=\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$ with
diagonal torus $T$ and standard basis $e_1,\dots,e_n$. Recall that an ordered
partition $\gamma=(S_1,\dots,S_r)$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ defines the coordinate
parabolic $P_\gamma=L_\gamma\ltimes U_\gamma$ of $G$, and that $L_\gamma$
depends only on the unordered collection of blocks, while $P_\gamma$ and
$U_\gamma$ depend on their order
([[def-coordinate-parabolics-for-ordered-partitions]]); for a composition
$\alpha$ this is the standard parabolic $P_\alpha=L_\alpha\ltimes U_\alpha$
([[def-compositions-partial-flags-and-standard-parabolics]],
[[thm-levi-decomposition-of-standard-parabolics-in-gl-n-fq]]).

1. **Transitivity.** Let $\delta$ and $\gamma$ be ordered partitions of
   $\{1,\dots,n\}$ such that every block of $\gamma$ is a union of blocks of
   $\delta$ and
   $\operatorname{blk}_\gamma(k)\le\operatorname{blk}_\gamma(l)$ whenever
   $\operatorname{blk}_\delta(k)<\operatorname{blk}_\delta(l)$ (that is, the
   order of the blocks of $\delta$ refines the order of the blocks of
   $\gamma$), so that
   $K:=L_\delta\le L:=L_\gamma$, $P_\delta=K\ltimes U_\delta\le P_\gamma=L\ltimes U_\gamma$
   and $U_\gamma\le U_\delta$. Then $L\cap P_\delta=K\ltimes(L\cap U_\delta)$ is a
   coordinate parabolic of $L$, and there are isomorphisms of functors
   $$R_K^{G,P_\delta}\;\cong\;R_L^{G,P_\gamma}\circ R_K^{L,L\cap P_\delta}, \qquad {}^*\!R_K^{G,P_\delta}\;\cong\;{}^*\!R_K^{L,L\cap P_\delta}\circ{}^*\!R_L^{G,P_\gamma},$$
   where each $R$ and ${}^*\!R$ is taken with respect to the displayed parabolic
   ([[def-harish-chandra-induction-and-restriction-for-finite-gl-n]]).
2. **Independence of the parabolic.** Let $\gamma=(S_1,\dots,S_r)$ be an ordered
   partition with blocks $S_1,\dots,S_r$ and let $\gamma'$ be the ordered
   partition obtained by listing the same blocks in another order, so that
   $L_{\gamma'}=L_\gamma=:L$ but $P_{\gamma'}$ need not equal $P_\gamma$. Then
   over $\mathbb C$ there are isomorphisms of functors on complex $L$-modules
   $$R_L^{G,P_\gamma}\;\cong\;R_L^{G,P_{\gamma'}}, \qquad {}^*\!R_L^{G,P_\gamma}\;\cong\;{}^*\!R_L^{G,P_{\gamma'}};$$
   equivalently, $R_L^{G,P_\gamma}W\cong R_L^{G,P_{\gamma'}}W$ for every complex
   $L$-module $W$, and $X^{U_\gamma}\cong X^{U_{\gamma'}}$ as $L$-modules for
   every complex $G$-module $X$. The isomorphisms are built from a choice of
   double-coset representatives and of isomorphisms on simple $L$-modules and
   need not be canonical; all the choices are finite.

claim_excerpt:
Input a real measurement matrix $A$ with $m$ rows indexed by $[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}$ and $d$ columns indexed by $k<d$, where $d\ge1$ and $m\ge0$. Use row $i-1$ of the ordinary zero-based $m\times d$ matrix for measurement label $i$. Input nonnegative intensities $b:[m]\to[0,\infty)$, a mode in $\{\mathrm{exact},\mathrm{noisy}\}$, a feasibility tolerance $\varepsilon\ge0$, a maximum sign-pattern count $P\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$, and a linear-solve budget $L\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$. Put $r_i=\sqrt{b_i}$.

For $m=0$, let $\mathcal S_m$ contain only the empty sign vector. For $m\ge1$, let
$$\mathcal S_m=\{s:[m]\to\{-1,+1\}:s_1=+1\},$$
ordered lexicographically with $+1$ before $-1$ and labels in increasing order. This gives one representative from each pair $\{s,-s\}$. A signed right-hand side is $y_s=(s_i r_i)_{i\in[m]}$, interpreted in the same zero-based row order as $A$.

If $P=0$ or $L=0$, return no candidates with status budget-exhausted. Otherwise compute one SVD of $A$, form its unique Moore–Penrose inverse $A^+$ and kernel $\ker A$, then process at most the first $P$ patterns in $\mathcal S_m$ and perform at most $L$ signed least-squares solves. Stop when either budget is exhausted. For each processed pattern $s$, compute the minimum-Euclidean-norm least-squares solution $x_s=A^+y_s$ and signed residual $e_s=\|Ax_s-y_s\|_2$. The budget $L$ counts right-hand-side solves after the one SVD factorization.

* In exact mode, record the affine family $x_s+\ker A$ when $e_s\le\varepsilon$, together with $e_s$. Mark it exact-feasible if $e_s=0$ and tolerance-feasible if $0<e_s\le\varepsilon$. If $\varepsilon=0$ and all patterns are processed, return the union of the exact-feasible families modulo $x\sim -x$, or report infeasible if this union is empty. For $\varepsilon>0$, report only the tolerance-qualified least-squares families; this is a tolerance screen, not a list of every vector whose residual is at most $\varepsilon$.
* In noisy mode, initialize the incumbent as unset. For the first processed pattern, store $x_s$ and $J(x_s)$. For each later processed pattern, replace the incumbent by $x_s$ exactly when $J(x_s)$ is strictly smaller than the incumbent value; on a tie, keep the earlier pattern.
  Compute each visited candidate's squared amplitude residual
  $$J(x_s)=\sum_{i\in[m]}(|(Ax_s)_i|-r_i)^2$$
  before applying that update. The feasibility tolerance is not used in this mode.
* Return the candidates and a status. Exact mode returns exact-feasible/infeasible only when $\varepsilon=0$ and all patterns are processed; positive tolerance returns tolerance-feasible/no-tolerance-fit when all patterns are processed. Noisy mode returns a completed best candidate when all patterns are processed. If either budget stops enumeration before all patterns are processed, return budget-exhausted with any candidates found. A budget-exhausted result makes no claim about unvisited patterns.

No statistical optimality or intensity-noise guarantee is part of this algorithm.
supplier_reference_lines: [[thm-least-squares-solutions-form-an-affine-kernel-translate-of-a-plus-b|Full affine least-squares solution family]]

claim_excerpt: Let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb R)$ and let $1\le r\le\min\{m,n\}$. Then $\operatorname{rank}A\ge r$ if and only if some $r$-rowed minor of $A$ is nonzero ([[def-submatrix-minors-of-a-rectangular-matrix]]). Equivalently, the rank of $A$ is the largest positive size of a nonzero minor when $A\ne0$, and it is $0$ when every entry is zero ([[cor-matrix-rank-equals-the-rank-of-its-linear-map]]).
supplier_reference_lines: [L2] A real $r\times r$ matrix has rank $r$ exactly when it is invertible, and it is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero ([[thm-invertible-matrix-theorem]], [[thm-real-square-matrix-invertible-iff-determinant-nonzero]]).

Let $r,N\ge1$ be integers and let $g_1,\ldots,g_N\in\mathbb R^r$. Define
$$
C=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i g_i:\lambda_i\ge0\text{ for every }i\right\}.
$$
Then $C$ is closed in the Euclidean topology, and for all $x,y\in C$ and all real $\alpha,\beta\ge0$, one has $\alpha x+\beta y\in C$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $q$ be a prime power. Put $G=\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$
and let $V=\mathbb F_q^n$. Then:

1. $G$ acts on the set $X$ of complete flags
   $0=F_0<F_1<\cdots<F_n=V$ with $\dim_{\mathbb F_q}F_i=i$ by
   $g\cdot F:=(\,g(F_0),\dots,g(F_n)\,)$;
2. the standard flag $V_\bullet$ with $V_i=\langle e_1,\dots,e_i\rangle$, where
   $e_1,\dots,e_n$ is the standard basis of $V$, is a complete flag whose
   stabiliser is the standard Borel subgroup $B$ of
   [[def-standard-subgroups-of-gl-n-over-a-finite-field]];
3. consequently $gB\mapsto g\cdot V_\bullet$ is a $G$-equivariant bijection
   $G/B\to X$, so the complete flags are in bijection with the left cosets of
   $B$.

claim_excerpt:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), as required by the
symplectic-basis, holomorphic-dimension, and wedge-period suppliers. Let $X$ be a
compact connected Riemann surface of genus $g$, with its complex orientation,
the fixed one-polygon symplectic basis $a_1,b_1,\ldots,a_g,b_g$ of
$H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$, and the fixed continuous side-loop representatives
$A_i,B_i$ supplied by
[[thm-symplectic-homology-basis-compact-riemann-surface]]. Let
$\Omega(X)=\Omega^1(X)$ be the $g$-dimensional complex vector space of
holomorphic differentials ([[lem-holomorphic-differentials-form-a-g-dimensional-space]]),
and let $P$ be the period pairing on this basis from
[[def-period-pairing-and-period-lattice]]. For closed smooth complex $1$-forms
when $g\ge1$, write $\Pi_\alpha$ and
$$S(\alpha,\beta):=\sum_{i=1}^g\bigl(\Pi_\alpha(a_i)\Pi_\beta(b_i)-\Pi_\alpha(b_i)\Pi_\beta(a_i)\bigr)$$
as in [[lem-cut-surface-and-boundary-jumps-of-primitives]] and
[[thm-symplectic-period-formula-for-wedge-integrals]]. For $g=0$ this sum is
empty. For a holomorphic $\omega$, the period lemma identifies
$\Pi_\omega(\gamma)=P(\gamma,\omega)$.

1. **Normalized basis.** The $\mathbb C$-linear map
   $$\mathcal A: \Omega(X)\longrightarrow\mathbb C^g, \qquad \omega\longmapsto(P(a_1,\omega),\ldots,P(a_g,\omega))$$
   is an isomorphism. Thus there is a unique basis
   $\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_g$ with $P(a_i,\omega_j)=\delta_{ij}$. The
   **period matrix** in this normalization is the $g\times g$ matrix
   $\Pi_{ij}:=P(b_i,\omega_j)$.
2. **First bilinear relation.** $\Pi$ is symmetric if and only if
   $S(\omega,\eta)=0$ for every pair of holomorphic differentials
   $\omega,\eta\in\Omega(X)$.
3. **Second bilinear relation.** $\operatorname{Im}\Pi$ is positive definite
   if and only if
   $$iS(\omega,\bar\omega)=i\int_X\omega\wedge\bar\omega>0$$
   for every nonzero holomorphic differential $\omega$. Here $\bar\omega$ is
   its conjugate smooth $(0,1)$-form.
4. **Period lattice.** The homomorphism
   $$e:H_1(X;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow\Omega(X)^*, \qquad e(\gamma)(\omega):=P(\gamma,\omega),$$
   is injective. Its image $\Lambda$ is the full lattice generated over
   $\mathbb Z$ by the $2g$ real-linearly independent vectors
   $e(a_1),e(b_1),\ldots,e(a_g),e(b_g)$. In the coordinates on $\Omega(X)^*$
   dual to the normalized basis,
   $$\Lambda=\mathbb Z^g+\Pi\mathbb Z^g\subseteq\mathbb C^g,$$
   and $\Omega(X)^*/\Lambda$ is a compact real $2g$-torus. For $g=0$, all
bases and matrices here are empty, $\Omega(X)=H_1(X;\mathbb Z)=0$, and we
use the rank-zero lattice convention $\Lambda=\{0\}$ in the zero vector
space; the quotient is a point. Positive definiteness of the empty matrix is
understood by the usual quadratic-form condition on nonzero vectors, which is
vacuous in dimension zero.
supplier_reference_lines: [[thm-invertible-matrix-theorem]]).

claim_excerpt:
Under the inputs and assumptions of the sample-based constrained policy
optimization update, with finite parameter dimension $d$ and nonnegative
integer backtracking budget $L$, the update has a unique mathematical output,
either `no-step` or an accepted parameter. Its proposals satisfy these properties.

If its matrix $H$ is symmetric positive definite and its local quadratic
program is feasible, the program has a nonempty compact global-maximizer set
and a unique lexicographically least global maximizer. This is the proposal
selected by the update and satisfies every linearized cost constraint and
the quadratic trust-region constraint.

If the program is infeasible with one cost and $u_1\ne0$, the inverse used
by the update exists, $a=u_1^TH^{-1}u_1>0$, and its recovery proposal is
$$ x^*=-\sqrt{2\delta/a}\,H^{-1}u_1. $$
It is the unique minimizer of $u_1^Tx$ on $\{x:x^THx/2\le\delta\}$,
satisfies $(x^*)^THx^*/2=\delta$, and decreases the linearized cost by
$\sqrt{2\delta a}$. It need not make the infeasible cost constraint feasible.
The non-positive-definite, zero-recovery-gradient and multiple-cost infeasible
branches return `no-step` as specified.

Once the specified exact subproblem decisions and operations have been
performed, backtracking terminates after at most $L+1$ candidate tests.
It returns the first passing candidate, which belongs to the parameter
domain and satisfies the empirical KL and all empirical cost tests, or
returns `no-step` if none passes. These are well-definedness and finite-search
properties of the exact mathematical update. They do not bound the cost of
exact feasibility/optimization operations or certify the true expected costs,
exact population KL, policy improvement, or convergence of sampled iterates.

claim_excerpt:
Let $d\ge1$ be an integer, let $t_1,\ldots,t_d$ be commuting indeterminates over $\mathbb R$, and let $V_d$ be the $d\times d$ matrix with $(i,j)$ entry $t_j^{i-1}$. Then
$$\det V_d=\prod_{1\le p<q\le d}(t_q-t_p).$$
Consequently, for any distinct real numbers $s_1,\ldots,s_d$, the $d$ vectors
$$(1,s_j,s_j^2,\ldots,s_j^{d-1})^{\mathsf T},\qquad 1\le j\le d,$$
are linearly independent.

Let $n\ge1$, let $q$ be a prime power, put $G=\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$
with standard Borel subgroup $B$, and for $g\in M_n(\mathbb F_q)$ and
$1\le i,j\le n$ let $r_{i,j}(g)$ denote the rank of the submatrix of $g$ on the
rows $i,i+1,\dots,n$ and the columns $1,2,\dots,j$
([[def-row-space-column-space-nullspace-and-matrix-ranks]]). Then:

1. $r_{i,j}(bg)=r_{i,j}(g)=r_{i,j}(gb)$ for all $b\in B$, so $r_{i,j}$ is
   constant on each double coset $BgB$;
2. if $g\in BwB$ for a permutation matrix $w=P_\sigma$
   ([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]), then
   $$r_{i,j}(g)=\#\{\,k\le j:\sigma(k)\ge i\,\};$$
3. for $g\in G$, triangular elimination supplies a permutation matrix
   with $g\in BP_\sigma B$
   ([[lem-gaussian-elimination-produces-a-pivot-permutation]]), and the rank matrix $(r_{i,j}(g))_{1\le i,j\le n}$ determines
   $\sigma$, and hence determines the double coset $BgB$, uniquely.

supplier_reference_lines: [L16] $M_n(S)$ denotes the square matrices over a commutative ring $S$, $AB$ the entrywise-sum matrix product, and $Vx$ the resulting matrix–vector product for $x\in S^n$; the determinant is the Leibniz sum $\det(V)=\sum_{\sigma}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}v_{\sigma(i),i}$, a finite signed sum of products of entries, so a matrix with entries in a subring $D\subseteq S$ has determinant in $D$; every solution $x$ of $Vx=w$ satisfies $\det(V)x_j=\det(V_j(w))$, where $V_j(w)$ is $V$ with column $j$ replaced by $w$ (Cramer's rule over a commutative ring); over a field $S$, a matrix $V\in M_n(S)$ is invertible exactly when the map $x\mapsto Vx$ has trivial kernel, and then $\det V$ is a unit of $S$ ([[def-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]], [[def-ring-matrix-product-identity-and-transpose]], [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]], [[thm-cramers-rule-over-a-commutative-ring]], [[thm-invertible-matrix-theorem]], [[cor-square-matrix-invertible-iff-determinant-is-a-unit]], [[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]]).

claim_excerpt:
**Ordered partitions.** An **ordered partition** of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is a finite
list $\gamma=(S_1,\dots,S_r)$ of nonempty pairwise disjoint subsets
$S_1,\dots,S_r\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}$ with
$S_1\cup\cdots\cup S_r=\{1,\dots,n\}$. Its members are the **blocks** of
$\gamma$, its **length** is $r$ (so that $1\le r\le n$ for $n\ge1$), and for
$1\le k\le n$ we write $\operatorname{blk}_\gamma(k)$ for the unique index with
$k\in S_{\operatorname{blk}_\gamma(k)}$, so that $k$ lies in an earlier block
than $l$ exactly when $\operatorname{blk}_\gamma(k)<\operatorname{blk}_\gamma(l)$.
A composition $\alpha=(a_1,\dots,a_r)$ of $n$ is the same datum as the ordered
partition $(I_1,\dots,I_r)$ whose blocks are its consecutive intervals
$I_i=\{\,d_{i-1}+1,\dots,d_i\,\}$
([[def-compositions-partial-flags-and-standard-parabolics]]); every ordered
partition is of this restricted form after relabelling, and the two notions are
compared below. The extreme ordered partitions are the one-block partition
$(\{1,\dots,n\})$ and the all-singleton partition
$(\{1\},\{2\},\dots,\{n\})$, which correspond to the compositions $(n)$ and
$(1^n)$.

**Coordinate parabolics.** Let $n\ge1$, let $q$ be a prime power, put
$G=\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$ with diagonal torus $T$ and standard basis
$e_1,\dots,e_n$ ([[def-standard-subgroups-of-gl-n-over-a-finite-field]]), and
let $\gamma=(S_1,\dots,S_r)$ be an ordered partition of $\{1,\dots,n\}$. Define
$$P_\gamma:=\{\,g\in G:g_{kl}=0\text{ whenever }\operatorname{blk}_\gamma(k)>\operatorname{blk}_\gamma(l)\,\},$$
$$L_\gamma:=\{\,g\in P_\gamma:g_{kl}=0\text{ whenever }\operatorname{blk}_\gamma(k)\ne\operatorname{blk}_\gamma(l)\,\},$$
$$U_\gamma:=\{\,g\in P_\gamma:g_{kk}=1\text{ for all }k,\text{ and }g_{kl}=0\text{ whenever }k\ne l\text{ and }\operatorname{blk}_\gamma(k)\ge\operatorname{blk}_\gamma(l)\,\},$$
the **coordinate parabolic**, its **coordinate Levi subgroup** and its
**coordinate unipotent radical** of type $\gamma$. For a composition $\alpha$
these are the standard subgroups $P_\alpha,L_\alpha,U_\alpha$ of
[[def-compositions-partial-flags-and-standard-parabolics]]. We also call
$$F^{(\gamma)}_i:=\langle e_j:j\in S_1\cup\cdots\cup S_i\rangle\qquad(0\le i\le r)$$
the **coordinate flag of type $\gamma$**, so that $F^{(\gamma)}_\bullet$ is a
strictly increasing chain of subspaces with
$\dim_{\mathbb F_q}F^{(\gamma)}_i=|S_1|+\cdots+|S_i|$, and $P_\gamma$ is the
stabiliser in $G$ of $F^{(\gamma)}_\bullet$: a matrix $p\in G$ satisfies
$p[F^{(\gamma)}_i]\subseteq F^{(\gamma)}_i$ for all $i$ exactly when, for every
$l$ with $\operatorname{blk}_\gamma(l)\le i$, the $l$-th column of $p$ has no
nonzero entry in a block $S_{i'}$ with $i'>i$, which is exactly
$p_{kl}=0$ whenever $\operatorname{blk}_\gamma(k)>\operatorname{blk}_\gamma(l)$
(the argument is that of
[[def-compositions-partial-flags-and-standard-parabolics]], where the same
computation is carried out for consecutive blocks, and it uses only the block
shape); since $p$ is injective and the chain is finite with
$\dim_{\mathbb F_q}p[F^{(\gamma)}_i]=\dim_{\mathbb F_q}F^{(\gamma)}_i$
([[thm-invertible-matrix-theorem]], [[def-linear-subspace]]), the inclusions are
equalities. In particular $P_\gamma$ is a subgroup of $G$, since the stabiliser
of a subset of the flag is a subgroup
([[def-subgroup]], [[def-group-action]]), and the diagonal torus satisfies
$T\le L_\gamma\le P_\gamma$.

**Change of coordinates.** Let $\sigma\in S_n$ and let
$u:=P_\sigma\in G$ be the associated permutation matrix
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]), so that
$(u^{-1}gu)_{ij}=g_{\sigma(i),\sigma(j)}$ for every matrix $g$
([[thm-matrix-multiplication-laws]],
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). For an ordered partition
$\gamma=(S_1,\dots,S_r)$ put $\sigma(\gamma):=(\sigma(S_1),\dots,\sigma(S_r))$,
again an ordered partition of $\{1,\dots,n\}$; then
$$\operatorname{blk}_{\sigma(\gamma)}(k)=\operatorname{blk}_\gamma(\sigma^{-1}(k))\qquad(1\le k\le n),$$
and applying the entry formula for conjugation to the three defining conditions
above gives
$$P_{\sigma(\gamma)}=uP_\gamma u^{-1},\qquad L_{\sigma(\gamma)}=uL_\gamma u^{-1},\qquad U_{\sigma(\gamma)}=uU_\gamma u^{-1}.$$
For instance $g\in uU_\gamma u^{-1}$ says that
$(u^{-1}gu)_{kk}=1$ and $(u^{-1}gu)_{kl}=0$ whenever $k\ne l$ and
$\operatorname{blk}_\gamma(k)\ge\operatorname{blk}_\gamma(l)$, which by the
displayed formula for $\operatorname{blk}_{\sigma(\gamma)}$ is the defining
condition for $U_{\sigma(\gamma)}$; the other two computations are identical.
Since a composition $\alpha$ is an ordered partition with consecutive blocks,
and since an arbitrary ordered partition $\gamma$ becomes a composition after
the relabelling that replaces every block by its position, the change of
coordinates shows that the coordinate parabolics of the ordered partitions are
exactly the conjugates $gP_\alpha g^{-1}$ of the standard parabolics by the
permutation matrices, and in particular they are split parabolic subgroups in
the sense of
[[def-harish-chandra-induction-and-restriction-for-finite-gl-n]].

**Consequences of the change of coordinates.** Fix an ordered partition
$\gamma=(S_1,\dots,S_r)$, choose the composition
$\alpha:=(|S_1|,\dots,|S_r|)$ of $n$, and let $\sigma\in S_n$ be the unique
permutation with $\sigma(I_i)=S_i$ for all $i$ that is increasing on each block
$I_i$; then $\gamma=\sigma(\alpha)$, and because
$P_\alpha=L_\alpha\ltimes U_\alpha$ with $U_\alpha\trianglelefteq P_\alpha$
([[thm-levi-decomposition-of-standard-parabolics-in-gl-n-fq]]), conjugation by
the permutation matrix $u=P_\sigma$ maps this decomposition to
$$P_\gamma=L_\gamma\ltimes U_\gamma,\qquad U_\gamma\trianglelefteq P_\gamma,\qquad L_\gamma\cap U_\gamma=\{I_n\},$$
because conjugation is an automorphism of $G$ and carries the block diagonal
matrices of type $\alpha$ onto those of type $\gamma$
([[cor-general-linear-group-is-a-group]], [[def-normal-subgroup]]); moreover
$P_\gamma$ is the stabiliser of the coordinate flag $F^{(\gamma)}_\bullet$, as
computed above. For the Weyl group, a permutation $\rho\in S_n$ satisfies
$\rho(S_i)=S_i$ for all $i$ exactly when $(\sigma^{-1}\rho\sigma)(I_i)=I_i$ for
all $i$, so with
$$W_\gamma:=\{\,\rho\in S_n:\rho(S_i)=S_i\text{ for every }1\le i\le r\,\}$$
one has $W_\gamma=\sigma W_\alpha\sigma^{-1}$ in the group $S_n$, where
$W_\alpha$ is the parabolic Weyl subgroup of
[[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]; combining that criterion with the
change of coordinates shows that a monomial matrix lies in $P_\gamma$ exactly
when its permutation lies in $W_\gamma$, so that
$$N\cap P_\gamma=T\cdot\{\,P_\rho:\rho\in W_\gamma\,\}$$
for the monomial subgroup $N$ of [[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]].
Finally, varying only the order of the blocks leaves the Levi unchanged: if
$\gamma'$ is obtained from $\gamma$ by permuting the list $(S_1,\dots,S_r)$,
then $\operatorname{blk}_{\gamma'}(k)\ne\operatorname{blk}_{\gamma'}(l)$ holds
exactly when $\operatorname{blk}_\gamma(k)\ne\operatorname{blk}_\gamma(l)$,
namely when $k,l$ lie in different blocks, so $L_{\gamma'}=L_\gamma$; the
unipotent radical $U_\gamma$ on the other hand depends on the order of the
blocks, as the case $r=2$ shows.

claim_excerpt: Let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}$, $d\ge1$, $m\ge0$, with rows labeled $i=1,\ldots,m$ and signal coordinates labeled $k<d$, and let $b:[m]\to[0,\infty)$. Denote row $i-1$ by $a_i$ and put $\Phi=(a_i)_{i\in[m]}$. Define $[x]$ using $x\sim -x$ and $\mathcal I_\Phi([x])=((Ax)_i^2)_{i\in[m]}$. Put $r_i=\sqrt{b_i}$. Use the sign set consisting of the empty pattern when $m=0$ and otherwise the patterns $s:[m]\to\{-1,+1\}$ with $s_1=+1$, ordered lexicographically with $+1$ before $-1$. For each pattern put $y_s=(s_i r_i)_{i\in[m]}$, let $x_s=A^+y_s$ be the minimum-norm least-squares solution, and let $e_s=\|Ax_s-y_s\|_2$. Here $A^+$ is the unique Moore–Penrose inverse and $\ker A=\{v:Av=0\}$. The algorithm processes patterns in order subject to a maximum pattern count $P\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ and signed-solve budget $L\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$; an early stop returns status budget-exhausted. Put $N_m=1$ for $m=0$ and $N_m=2^{m-1}$ for $m\ge1$. The procedure terminates after no more than $P$, $L$, or $N_m$ signed solves, whichever bound is reached first; if $P,L>0$ it computes one SVD, and full pattern processing uses exactly $N_m$ signed solves. Thus the pattern count grows exponentially in $m$ for $m\ge1$. In exact mode with tolerance $\varepsilon=0$, after every pattern is processed it returns the union of the exact families $x_s+\ker A$ modulo global sign, or reports infeasible if that union is empty. For every processed pattern, $x_s$ minimizes $\|Ax-y_s\|_2$, and the complete set of signed least-squares minimizers is $x_s+\ker A$; this set solves $Ax=y_s$ exactly if and only if its residual $e_s$ is zero. The complete exact-mode output is exactly $\{[x]:\mathcal I_\Phi([x])=b\}$. In noisy mode the algorithm scores $J(x)=\sum_{i\in[m]}(|(Ax)_i|-r_i)^2$ and, after every canonical pattern is processed, returns a candidate minimizing $J$ over all $x\in\mathbb R^d$. Whenever at least one pattern is processed in noisy mode, its returned incumbent minimizes $J$ among the processed candidates. When a budget stops enumeration early, the returned candidates describe only processed patterns and give no completeness or global-minimum guarantee. For $m=0$, the single pattern has the unique empty right-hand side and $J(x)=0$ for every $x$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $q$ be a prime power and let $\alpha=(a_1,\dots,a_r)$ be a
composition of $n$, with standard parabolic $P_\alpha$, standard Levi subgroup
$L_\alpha$ and standard unipotent radical $U_\alpha$
([[def-compositions-partial-flags-and-standard-parabolics]]). Then $L_\alpha$
and $U_\alpha$ are subgroups of $P_\alpha$, $L_\alpha\cap U_\alpha=\{I_n\}$,
$U_\alpha\trianglelefteq P_\alpha$, and the multiplication map
$$L_\alpha\times U_\alpha\longrightarrow P_\alpha,\qquad (l,u)\longmapsto lu,$$
is a bijection; equivalently
$$P_\alpha=L_\alpha\ltimes U_\alpha .$$
Moreover the block diagonal map is an isomorphism of groups
$$L_\alpha\longrightarrow \operatorname{GL}_{a_1}(\mathbb F_q)\times\cdots\times\operatorname{GL}_{a_r}(\mathbb F_q),\qquad l\longmapsto(A_{11},\dots,A_{rr}),$$
whose inverse assembles the blocks, and the two extreme cases are
$P_{(n)}=G=L_{(n)}$, $U_{(n)}=\{I_n\}$ and $P_{(1^n)}=B=L_{(1^n)}\ltimes U_{(1^n)}$
with $L_{(1^n)}=T$ the diagonal torus and $U_{(1^n)}=U$ the standard maximal
unipotent subgroup.

claim_excerpt:
Let $\mathbb H$ be the quaternions with conjugate $x\mapsto\bar x$ and norm $N$,
let $S^3=\{q\in\mathbb H:N(q)=1\}$ be the unit sphere, and let
$\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H=\mathbb Ri\oplus\mathbb Rj\oplus\mathbb Rk$ carry the
restricted Euclidean inner product, identified with $\mathbb R^3$ through the
basis $(i,j,k)$. Let $\operatorname{SO}(3)$ be the group of real $3\times3$
matrices $R$ with $R^{\mathsf T}R=I$ and $\det R=1$, carrying the subspace
topology of the nine entries, and for $q\in S^3$ let $\rho(q)$ be the linear map
of $\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H$ defined by
$$\rho(q)(v)=qvq^{-1},$$
written in the basis $(i,j,k)$ as a real $3\times3$ matrix. Then:

1. $\rho:S^3\to\operatorname{SO}(3)$ is a continuous surjective group
   homomorphism with kernel $\{\pm1\}$, and it is a two-sheeted covering map;
   consequently $\operatorname{SO}(3)$ is homeomorphic to the orbit space
   $S^3/\{\pm1\}$.
2. For every covering $p:E\to B$, every $e_0\in E$ and every integer $n\ge2$,
   the induced homomorphism $p_*:\pi_n(E,e_0)\to\pi_n(B,p(e_0))$ is an
   isomorphism. In particular
   $\rho_*:\pi_3(S^3,1)\to\pi_3(\operatorname{SO}(3),I)$ is an isomorphism.
3. $\pi_3(S^3,1)\cong\mathbb Z$ by degree, and $\rho_*$ carries the degree-one
   generator of $\pi_3(S^3,1)$ to the class $[\rho]$; hence
   $\pi_3(\operatorname{SO}(3),I)\cong\mathbb Z$ is generated by $[\rho]$.
4. The clutching construction over the equatorial $S^3$ with clutching map
   $\rho$ produces an oriented rank-three real vector bundle
   $E_\rho\to S^4$ which is not trivial.

claim_excerpt:
Let $A:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ solve the variational equation

$$A'(t)=C(t)A(t),\qquad A(t_0)=I_n,$$

on an interval $I$, where $C:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ is continuous. Then every
matrix $A(t)$ is invertible. Equivalently, a fundamental matrix of the
variational equation is invertible at every time on its interval of definition.
supplier_reference_lines: [L3] A finite square matrix is invertible if and only if its nullspace is zero; this includes the empty matrix ([[thm-invertible-matrix-theorem]]).

claim_excerpt:
Let $n\ge 1$, let $A\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb{R})$, let
$\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_n>0$ be its singular values, and let
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ be the spectral (operator) norm. Then:

1. **Smallest singular value as a minimum.**
   $\sigma_n=\min\{\lVert Ax\rVert_2:\lVert x\rVert_2=1\}$.
2. **Distance to singularity.**
   $$\min\Bigl\{\lVert E\rVert_2\;:\;E\in M_n(\mathbb{R}),\ A+E\text{ is singular}\Bigr\}=\sigma_n,$$
   and the minimum is attained.
3. **Relative distance.**
   $$\frac{\min_{A+E\text{ singular}}\lVert E\rVert_2}{\lVert A\rVert_2}=\frac{\sigma_n}{\sigma_1}=\frac{1}{\kappa_2(A)},$$
   where $\kappa_2(A)$ is the condition number of
   [[def-condition-number-of-a-nonsingular-linear-system]]. Equivalently,
   $\lVert A^{-1}\rVert_2=1/\sigma_n$.

In words: the nearest singular matrix to $A$ lies at spectral distance
$\sigma_n$, and that distance relative to the scale $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$
is exactly $1/\kappa_2(A)$.
supplier_reference_lines: [L4] A square matrix is invertible exactly when it has rank $n$ ([[thm-invertible-matrix-theorem]]).

claim_excerpt:
Let $n\ge1$ and let $T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be linear, with standard matrix $A$. For every bounded Jordan set $E$, the image $T(E)$ is a bounded Jordan set and
$$\operatorname{cont}(T(E))=|\det A|\operatorname{cont}(E).$$
In particular, a singular linear image has content zero.
supplier_reference_lines: [L6] Every finite matrix over a field is row equivalent, by Gaussian elimination, to a matrix in row echelon form ([[thm-gaussian-elimination-produces-row-echelon-form]]). For $A\in M_n(F)$, the matrix $A$ is invertible if and only if it has a pivot in every row and every column ([[thm-invertible-matrix-theorem]]).
